newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Armenian army in streets as opposition lies low.
newsitem.headline: Armenian army in streets as opposition lies low.

text.p: Thousands of troops backed by armoured vehicles patrolled the centre of the Armenian capital Yerevan for a second day on Friday following President Levon Ter-Petrosyan's disputed election victory.

Rival presidential candidate Vazgen Manukyan, whose supporters clashed with riot police outside parliament on Wednesday, has accused Ter-Petrosyan of rigging the poll. International observers noted irregularities.
Ter-Petrosyan called the clashes, in which some protesters entered the parliament and assaulted the speaker and his deputy, an attempted "fascist" coup by "mentally ill people".

Paruir Hayrikyan, a leading opposition figure who spent more than 17 years in Soviet labour camps, told reporters on Friday that the government had arrested around 100 political opponents since a crackdown began following the unrest.
Other opposition activists have gone into hiding after Ter-Petrosyan sealed off the headquarters of several political parties, including Manukyan's National Democratic Union.

Ter-Petrosyan aide Jerair Liparityan could not confirm or deny Hayrikyan's allegations. "The Prosecutor General will be issuing information on exactly how many people have been arrested and what the charges are," he told Reuters.

An interior ministry spokesman said Manukyan had not been arrested. Several other opposition parliament members were detained on Thursday after the chamber voted to lift their immunity for allegedly leading the clashes.
"Until the Central Electoral Commission gives us permission we cannot detain him," the interior ministry spokesman added.
The commission says that, as a presidential candidate, Manukyan has special immunity from arrest until Sunday.
Manukyan's wife Darduhi said at a clandestine meeting with reporters her husband had left Yerevan and was in hiding. She did not know his exact whereabouts but he was not under arrest.
She read out a statement from the 50-year-old physicist in which he called Ter-Petrosyan's rule "an illegal regime".

Liparityan dismissed the charge and defended using the army to maintain order. "He can say whatever he likes. If people in Washington would have tried to enter the Capitol building and beat up Gingrich, they would have been shot," he said, referring to House of Representatives speaker Newt Gingrich.
Some opposition figures accuse Ter-Petrosyan of deliberately provoking the trouble to justify a crackdown on opponents.
But Manukyan, who went to the parliament to negotiate with the head of the Central Electoral Commission, told supporters to come in after him if he did not emerge after half an hour.
Manukyan, Ter-Petrosyan's former prime minister, says he won Sunday's election. Unofficial results gave Ter-Petrosyan 52 percent of the vote compared with only 41 percent for Manukyan.

The streets of Yerevan remained tense on Friday, with soldiers blocking off main streets and squares. State radio has been broadcasting solemn patriotic music and information while two independent stations have gone off the air.

Ter-Petrosyan, 50, has led this small Caucasus country of 3.5 million since independence in 1991, a period marked by economic hardship and confrontation with neighbouring Azerbaijan over the disputed enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh.
Conditions have eased in recent months as the economy begins to rebound but Armenia has suffered many winters of power cuts and shortages.
